subject: St Benedict of Nursia, also called Benedict of Norcia, abbot of Monte Cassino

text_used.text: Two texts carry almost everything. (1) His life: Gregory the Great, Dialogues Book 2, the only early Life, in the 1608 English of 'P.W.' re-edited by Edmund G. Gardner (1911), fetched whole from tertullian.org (sources/people/benedict-of-nursia/gregory-dialogues-book2-pw1608-gardner1911.txt), with the Latin from la.wikisource (gregory-dialogues-book2-latin-wikisource.txt). (2) His own words: the Rule. For the page's own quotations the Rule is quoted from Boniface Verheyen's translation on CCEL (rule-verheyen-ccel.txt), because CCEL has one readable page per chapter. The quiz's shown lines keep the editions they were checked in: Hunter Blair (1906) for 'laugh' and 'tell', Henderson (1892) for 'quiet'; both scans were fetched whole and matched. 'exact' is the translation as printed (footnote numbers and page markers taken out). 'display' applies the site's rule of capitals for every pronoun for God. Latin of the Rule: The Latin Library (rule-latin-thelatinlibrary.txt).
text_used.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain; Boniface Verheyen (tr., d. 1923), The Holy Rule of St. Benedict, CCEL plain text marked Public Domain; D. Oswald Hunter Blair (tr.), The Rule of St. Benedict (Fort Augustus, imprimatur 21 March 1906; archive.org lists 1907), archive.org OCR, marked Public Domain Mark; Ernest F. Henderson (tr.), Select Historical Documents of the Middle Ages (London: George Bell, 1892), archive.org (Cornell copy)
text_used.note: Gardner's text keeps the 1608 spelling (strake, bad for bade, holden). One misprint: chapter 23 reads 'his heart conversed to above in heaven' (read: 'so above'); do not quote that line without checking a scan. P.W. calls the bird of chapter 8 a 'crow'; Gregory's Latin says corvus (a raven). CCEL pages: chapter N of the Rule is rule.<roman numeral N+2>.html (prologue rule.ii.html), each fetched and its heading checked. Verheyen's CCEL header says '1949 Edition', translator 1844-1923, Rights: Public Domain. Doyle's 1948 translation (Gutenberg 50040) is copyrighted outside the US: not used.

born_year.text: About 480. Gregory gives no year. The date is traditional.
born_year.source: Catholic Encyclopedia 1907 ('born at Nursia, c. 480'); Merriam-Webster ('Saint circa 480-circa 547'); Gardner's note 1 ('born at Nursia about 480'); Britannica ('born c. 480 ce'); Orthodox Encyclopedia ('ок. 480')
born_year.note: Wikidata's 480-03-04 is not in any source read. saint.gr gives 481. Say 'about 480'.

born_place.text: In 'the province of Nursia', of a good family. Nursia is today Norcia, in Umbria, Italy.
born_place.source: Dialogues 2, prologue ('He was born in the province of Nursia, of honourable parentage'); Latin 'liberiori genere ex prouincia Nursiae exortus'; Britannica ('Nursia [Italy]'; also known as 'Saint Benedict of Norcia'); Orthodox Encyclopedia ('совр. Норча, обл. Умбрия')
born_place.note: The Catholic Encyclopedia calls him 'the son of a Roman noble'; Gregory says only 'honourable parentage' (Latin: 'of freer birth').

grew_up.text: He was sent to Rome to study. He left the schools because he saw fellow students fall into 'dissolute and lewd life'.
grew_up.source: Dialogues 2, prologue ('brought up at Rome in the study of humanity')
grew_up.note: His age then is disputed. The OCA and azbyka say he was sent to Rome at fourteen. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1907): 'It has been very generally stated as fourteen, but a careful examination of St. Gregory's narrative makes it impossible to suppose him younger than nineteen or twenty.' It dates his leaving Rome 'at about A.D. 500'.

died.text: At Monte Cassino, of a fever, six days after he had his grave opened. He died standing in the oratory, held up by his monks, praying with his hands raised, just after receiving communion. The day kept is 21 March. The year is about 547 (some say 543).
died.source: Dialogues 2, chapter 37; Calendarium Romanum 1969 ('Memoria S. Benedicti († die 21 martii 547)'; 'Depositio S. Benedicti in Monte Cassino die 21 martii 547 ab aliquibus manuscriptis Martyrologii hieronymiani et a Martyrologio Bedae recolitur'); Merriam-Webster (circa 547); Britannica (c. 547); OCA (547); Catholic Encyclopedia 1907 (543)
died.note: Gregory gives neither day nor year. 543 is the Catholic Encyclopedia's, Gardner's tradition ('St. Benedict a month later, March 21, 543'), saint.gr's and the Episcopal Church's ('c. 543'). The Church of England prints 'c.550'. The Episcopal essay: 'He died sometime between 540 and 550'. Plain wording: 'about 547; some say 543'.

buried.text: In the oratory of St John the Baptist at Monte Cassino, which he had built where Apollo's altar stood, in the grave he had already given his sister Scholastica.
buried.note: Where the relics are now is disputed: the Catholic Encyclopedia (1907) says 'There is some doubt whether the relics of the saint are still at Monte Cassino, or whether they were moved in the seventh century to Fleury', and reports Abbot Tosti's case for Monte Cassino. Pope Paul VI (1964) calls the Monte Cassino church 'famous for the tomb of St Benedict' ('ob eiusdem Sancti Benedicti sepulchrum celeberrimam').

also_called.source: Britannica ('Also known as: Saint Benedict of Norcia, Saint Benedict of Nursia')

also_called.text: Father of Western monasticism. The Church of England prints him as 'Benedict of Nursia, Abbot of Monte Cassino, Father of Western Monasticism'.
also_called.source: Church of England, Common Worship calendar; Britannica ('father of Western monasticism'); Catholic Encyclopedia ('Founder of western monasticism')

also_called.text: 'Venerable Benedict of Nursia' in the OCA; 'Όσιος Βενέδικτος ο εκ Νουρσίας' (Venerable Benedict of Nursia) in Greek; 'Преподобный Венедикт Нурсийский' (Venedikt) in Russian. 'Venerable' is the Orthodox title for a monk saint.

also_called.source: Paul VI, Pacis nuntius, 24 October 1964: 'Sanctum Benedictum Abbatem totius Europae principalem apud Deum caelestem Patronum constituimus ac declaramus'

also_called.text: His name means blessed: Gregory opens, 'blessed by grace, and blessed in name, for he was called "Benedictus" or Benedict'.

status.text: A saint to Catholics and to the Orthodox. The Church of England keeps him as a Lesser Festival; the Episcopal Church and the ELCA remember him on 11 July. The Missouri Synod's calendar does not list him.
status.source: USCCB; OCA; saint.gr; Church of England; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022; Evangelical Lutheran Worship; CPH list of LSB commemorations

patron_of.text: Europe: Pope Paul VI named him principal patron of all Europe on 24 October 1964, the day he consecrated the rebuilt church of Monte Cassino. Britannica adds: 'He is also a patron of students and monastics, and he is invoked as a protector against poisoning and kidney disease.'
patron_of.source: Paul VI, Pacis nuntius (AAS 56 (1964), pp. 965-967); Britannica
patron_of.note: The vatican.va page title reads 'Die 29 m. Octobris', but the letter itself is dated 'die XXIV mensis Octobris, anno MCMLXIV'. Use 24 October 1964 (also Britannica's 1964). Wikidata lists 63 patronages: unverified, not used.

in_art.text: An abbot in a black habit, with a book (his Rule) and an abbot's staff.
in_art.source: Orthodox Encyclopedia, 'Iconography' ('с характерных атрибутов святого (книга, посох и др.)'); the Memling panel (Uffizi) shows him reading, with a crozier

in_art.text: A broken cup or glass and a raven with bread: the poisoned wine and the poisoned loaf of Gregory's chapters 3 and 8.
in_art.source: Catholic Encyclopedia 1912, 'Medal of Saint Benedict' ('On the one side of the image is a cup, on the other a raven'); Rijksmuseum print RP-P-BI-504 titled 'Heilige Benedictus als abt met kromstaf en gebroken kelk en raaf met brood' (as abbot with crozier and broken chalice and raven with bread)
in_art.note: The Rijksmuseum title was read from its Commons file name only.

in_art.text: In the East: a monk with a white beard and a scroll, as in the 16th-century fresco at the Patriarchate of Peć, inscribed 'СТЫИ ВЕНЕДИКТЪ' (Holy Benedict).
in_art.source: The Peć fresco (Commons); inscription read from the picture
in_art.note: The Orthodox Encyclopedia shows a 20th-century Russian icon; no pre-20th-century Eastern icon of him was found on Commons besides Peć.

in_art.text: The story most painted: the cave at Subiaco, with Romanus lowering bread on a rope and the devil breaking the bell.
in_art.source: Master of Messkirch, about 1530, Staatsgalerie Stuttgart (the band picture); Master of St Wolfgang, hand-coloured woodcut, about 1440-1450, NGA 8750

wrote.text: One work that is surely his: the Rule for monks, in a prologue and 73 short chapters. Gregory calls it 'excellent for discretion and also eloquent for the style'.
wrote.source: Catholic Encyclopedia ('eleven chapters out of the seventy-three of his Rule'); Dialogues 2, chapter 36; the Rule's own chapter list (Hunter Blair, Verheyen)
wrote.note: Nothing else he wrote survives. Britannica: 'The only recognized authority for the facts of Benedict's life is book 2 of the Dialogues'.

roles.text: Student: sent to Rome for his schooling; he left the schools 'instructed with learned ignorance, and furnished with unlearned wisdom'.
Hermit: three years alone in a cave at Subiaco, fed by the monk Romanus.
Abbot: of a monastery near Subiaco (said to be Vicovaro), then of twelve small monasteries of twelve monks each.
roles.note: Vicovaro is tradition ('is said to have been'), not Gregory.

roles.text: Founder: of Monte Cassino, built about 529 on a hill where Apollo was still worshipped.
roles.source: Dialogues 2, chapter 8; Gardner's note 17 ('in 528 or 529'); Orthodox Encyclopedia ('ок. 529 г.'); Lesser Feasts and Fasts ('Sometime between 525 and 530')

roles.text: Lawgiver: author of the Rule, which Western monks and nuns still follow.

catholic.text: 11 July, a memorial in the General Roman Calendar ('Memorial of Saint Benedict, Abbot').
catholic.source: USCCB readings for 11 July 2025 (Wayback copy of 10 Feb 2026; USCCB answers 403 to the checker directly); Calendarium Romanum 1969 ('11 S. Benedicti, abbatis Memoria')

roman_martyrology_1916.text: 21 March: 'At Mount Cassino, the birthday of the holy abbot Benedict, who restored and wonderfully extended in the West the monastic discipline, which was almost destroyed. His life, brilliant in virtues and miracles, was written by pope St. Gregory.' The 1916 Martyrology has nothing for him on 11 July.
roman_martyrology_1916.source: The Roman Martyrology (1916), 21 March (the entry between 'the Twentieth Day' (St Joachim) and 'the Twenty-second Day' (St Paul of Narbonne)); 11 July read whole
roman_martyrology_1916.note: Its own footnote defines a saint's 'birthday' as the day of entering heaven (see Martin's facts).

orthodox.text: 14 March in the Greek churches and the OCA. The Russian Church keeps 14 March on the old calendar, which is 27 March on today's calendar.
orthodox.source: OCA ('Venerable Benedict of Nursia', listed on 14 March); saint.gr ('Εορτάζει στις 14 Μαρτίου εκάστου έτους'); Romfea ('14 Μαρτίου - Άγιος Βενέδικτος ο εκ Νουρσίας'); azbyka.ru ('День памяти 27 марта'); Orthodox Encyclopedia ('пам. 14 мар.')
orthodox.note: GOARCH answered 403 to the checker, as for Martin and Antony.

anglican.text: 11 July, a Lesser Festival in the Church of England: 'Benedict of Nursia, Abbot of Monte Cassino, Father of Western Monasticism, c.550'.
anglican.source: Church of England, Common Worship calendar (printed in roman type, which the calendar's key says marks a Lesser Festival; Scholastica on 10 February is in italic, a Commemoration)

episcopal.source: Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 (calendar and pages 305-306)

lutheran.text: ELCA: 11 July, 'Benedict of Nursia, Abbot of Monte Cassino, c. 540'. The Missouri Synod's list of commemorations (Lutheran Service Book) has no entry for him.
lutheran.source: Evangelical Lutheran Worship, 'The Church Year' (final draft, 2006, Wayback); CPH list of LSB commemorations (July: Isaiah, Ruth, Elijah, Ezekiel, Bach, Mary Martha and Lazarus, Barnes, Joseph of Arimathea)
lutheran.note: The ELW source is the published final draft, as for Antony.

why_the_dates_differ.text: 21 March is the traditional day of his death, recorded by some manuscripts of the Hieronymian Martyrology and by Bede's Martyrology, and kept at Rome from the 11th century. A July feast called 'Natalis S. Benedicti' appears in liturgical books written in Gaul at the end of the 8th century; its origin is not known. In 1969 Rome moved his memorial to 11 July because 21 March always falls in Lent. Monks still keep 21 March too, says Britannica. The Byzantine calendar has had 14 March since the 10th-century Synaxarion of Constantinople and the Typikon of the Great Church; some south-Italian Greek books kept 21 March.
why_the_dates_differ.source: Calendarium Romanum 1969 (commentary for 11 July and for 21 March); Britannica ('Benedict's feast day is kept by monks on March 21, the traditional day of his death, and by the Roman Catholic Church on July 11'); Orthodox Encyclopedia (Byzantine calendars)
why_the_dates_differ.note: Exact Latin (OCR): 'Memoria S. Benedicti (f die 21 martii 547), cum semper in Quadragesima occurrat, die 11 iulii reponitur, qua die in multis regionibus a saeculo vm celebratur' ('vm' is VIII, '(f' is †). No source says why the East chose 14 March. The popular claim that 11 July marks the moving of his relics to Fleury is not what the 1969 calendar says ('quamvis de origine huius festi compertum non sit').

numbers.text: 3: years he lived hidden in the cave at Subiaco, 'unknown to all men, except to Romanus'.
12 x 12: the monasteries he built at Subiaco, twelve of them, 'and in each of them placed twelve monks'.
73: chapters in his Rule, after a prologue.
150: psalms his monks sang every week. He sighs that the old fathers did 'in one day what we lukewarm monks should, please God, perform at least in a week'.
2: people raised from the dead in Gregory's Life, a young monk crushed by a wall and a farmer's little son.
1 hemina: the wine allowed each monk a day (Hunter Blair: 'one pint'), because 'monks in our times cannot be persuaded' to give it up.
numbers.note: A hemina is about half a litre; Hunter Blair renders it 'one pint'. Do not print a litre figure without a source.

numbers.text: 200: bushels of flour found in sacks at his door in a famine, the day after he promised plenty.
3: times the Rule is read aloud to a newcomer over his first year (after 2 months, 6 more months and 4 more), before he may promise to stay.
numbers.note: Britannica: 'his establishment of a full year's probation'.

numbers.text: 1964: the year he was named patron of all Europe.

traits.title: calm with the men who tried to kill him
traits.text: His monks near Subiaco put poison in his wine. When the glass shattered at his blessing, he stood up calmly, forgave them and left. Later a jealous priest sent him a poisoned loaf; Gregory says Benedict grieved for the priest more than for himself.

quote.exact: with a mild countenance and quiet mind, he called the monks together, and spake thus unto them: "Almighty God have mercy upon you, and forgive you: why have you used me in this manner?
quote.display: with a mild countenance and quiet mind, he called the monks together, and spake thus unto them: "Almighty God have mercy upon you, and forgive you: why have you used me in this manner?
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

also.exact: was far more sorry for him than grieved for himself
also.display: was far more sorry for him than grieved for himself
also.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

also.exact: he gave him penance, for that, sending such news, he presumed to rejoice at his enemy's death
also.display: he gave him penance, for that, sending such news, he presumed to rejoice at his enemy's death
also.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain
also.note: When the priest Florentius was killed by his own falling room, Benedict wept, and gave a penance to the monk who sent the news gladly.

traits.title: hard to rattle
traits.text: A Goth named Galla, who killed any monk he met, came raging after a bound farmer and shouted at Benedict to get up. Benedict looked up from his book, and the ropes fell off the farmer's arms. Galla fell at his feet. Benedict stayed seated and told his monks to feed him.

quote.exact: the venerable man for all this rose not up from his reading
quote.display: the venerable man for all this rose not up from his reading
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain
quote.note: Latin: 'vir sanctus a lectione minime surrexit'.

traits.title: quick to anger at disobedience
traits.text: In a famine he had given everything away. When his cellarer kept back the last glass of oil instead of giving it to a man who asked, Benedict had it thrown out of the window. He also struck a wandering monk with a stick, and once in anger told a restless monk to go.

quote.exact: Then in an anger he commanded others to take that glass with the oil, and to throw it out at the window, to the end that nothing might remain in the Abbey contrary to obedience.
quote.display: Then in an anger he commanded others to take that glass with the oil, and to throw it out at the window, to the end that nothing might remain in the Abbey contrary to obedience.
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

also.exact: whom for the blindness of his heart he strake with a little wand
also.display: whom for the blindness of his heart he strake with a little wand
also.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

also.exact: wearied with his importunity, in anger bad him depart
also.display: wearied with his importunity, in anger bad him depart
also.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

traits.title: sober, not tearful
traits.text: A friend once found him weeping hard, and was surprised. Gregory explains why.

quote.exact: for the man of God used not in his prayers to weep, but rather to be sad
quote.display: for the man of God used not in his prayers to weep, but rather to be sad
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain
quote.note: He wept because he foresaw his abbey would be sacked; Gregory says the Lombards later sacked it but killed no one.

traits.title: moderate on purpose
traits.text: He wanted a rule a beginner could live. His Rule promises nothing harsh, lets monks drink a little wine, and tells the abbot to go gently.

quote.exact: We are, therefore, about to found a school of the Lord's service, in which we hope to introduce nothing harsh or burdensome.
quote.display: We are, therefore, about to found a school of the Lord's service, in which we hope to introduce nothing harsh or burdensome.
quote.source: Boniface Verheyen (tr., d. 1923), The Holy Rule of St. Benedict, CCEL plain text marked Public Domain

also.exact: let him so temper everything that the strong may still have something to desire and the weak may not draw back
also.display: let him so temper everything that the strong may still have something to desire and the weak may not draw back
also.source: Boniface Verheyen (tr., d. 1923), The Holy Rule of St. Benedict, CCEL plain text marked Public Domain

traits.title: did not take credit for wonders
traits.text: When Maurus ran across the lake to save young Placidus, Benedict said it was Maurus's obedience. When a father begged him to raise his son, he first protested that such miracles belong to the apostles.

quote.exact: the venerable man did not attribute this to his own merits, but to the obedience of Maurus
quote.display: the venerable man did not attribute this to his own merits, but to the obedience of Maurus
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

also.exact: Away, my good brethren, away: such miracles are not for us to work, but for the blessed Apostles: why will you lay such a burthen upon me, as my weakness cannot bear?
also.display: Away, my good brethren, away: such miracles are not for us to work, but for the blessed Apostles: why will you lay such a burthen upon me, as my weakness cannot bear?
also.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

traits.title: ran from praise
traits.text: His first miracle made him famous in the village. So he slipped away from his old nurse and went alone into the wild.

quote.exact: desiring rather the miseries of the world than the praises of men: rather to be wearied with labour for God's sake, than to be exalted with transitory commendation
quote.display: desiring rather the miseries of the world than the praises of men: rather to be wearied with labour for God's sake, than to be exalted with transitory commendation
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

traits_note: Seven traits, each shown by what he did, as the rule of 2026-09-25 allows ('the person shapes the page'). The first two back the site's Oak card. The stern side (the third) must stay beside the gentle side: both are Gregory's.

others_on_him.display: who, from his younger years, carried always the mind of an old man; for his age was inferior to his virtue
others_on_him.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

others_on_him.note: Latin: 'ab ipso suae pueritiae tempore cor gerens senile'.

others_on_him.display: for he wrote a rule for his monks, both excellent for discretion and also eloquent for the style.

others_on_him.display: for the holy man could not otherwise teach, than himself lived.

others_on_him.exact: this one man was full of the spirit of all good men.
others_on_him.display: this one man was full of the spirit of all good men.
others_on_him.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

others_on_him.exact: the birthday of the holy abbot Benedict, who restored and wonderfully extended in the West the monastic discipline, which was almost destroyed. His life, brilliant in virtues and miracles, was written by pope St. Gregory.
others_on_him.display: the birthday of the holy abbot Benedict, who restored and wonderfully extended in the West the monastic discipline, which was almost destroyed. His life, brilliant in virtues and miracles, was written by pope St. Gregory.
others_on_him.check: word for word (punctuation or quote marks differ, or OCR line breaks)

others_on_him_note: No one who knew him wrote about him. Gregory (pope 590-604) says he could not learn 'all the notable things' and names his four informants: Constantinus and Simplicius (the next abbots of Monte Cassino), Valentinianus (for many years abbot of the Lateran monastery) and Honoratus (abbot of Subiaco when Gregory wrote). The Dialogues are traditionally dated 593-94 (DeGregorio, The Medieval Review 04.10.14). Pope Paul VI (1964) opens his letter 'Pacis nuntius, unitatis effector, civilis cultus magister' (Our translation: 'Messenger of peace, maker of unity, teacher of civilised life'); Latin verified in pacis-nuntius-1964-latin.txt. The Vatican's English is copyrighted, so any English must be marked 'Our translation'.

life_moments.title: Walking out of school
life_moments.text: He saw many students in Rome fall into loose living, so he gave up his books and left home. His old nurse would not leave him, and they lived at Enfide (today Affile). There she borrowed a sieve and it broke in two. She wept, because it was not hers. He prayed over the pieces and it was whole. The village hung it over the church door, and it was still there in Gregory's day.

quote.exact: and in this sort he departed, instructed with learned ignorance, and furnished with unlearned wisdom.
quote.display: and in this sort he departed, instructed with learned ignorance, and furnished with unlearned wisdom.
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain
quote.note: Latin: 'Recessit igitur scienter nesciens, et sapienter indoctus.' The year 500 is the Catholic Encyclopedia's estimate, not Gregory's. Affile: Gardner's note 2 and Britannica.

life_moments.title: The bread on a rope
life_moments.text: He fled from his nurse to a narrow cave in the rocks at Subiaco, about forty miles from Rome. Only one monk, Romanus, knew he was there. Romanus saved bread from his own meals and let it down over the cliff on a long rope with a little bell tied on, so Benedict would hear it coming. The devil threw a stone and broke the bell, but Romanus kept coming.

quote.exact: upon a long rope, did let down the loaf, upon which also with a band he tied a little bell, that by the ringing thereof the man of God might know when he came with his bread
quote.display: upon a long rope, did let down the loaf, upon which also with a band he tied a little bell, that by the ringing thereof the man of God might know when he came with his bread
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

life_moments.title: He did not know it was Easter
life_moments.text: God told a priest far away that he was feasting while His servant went hungry. The priest found the cave on Easter Day and said it was time to eat. Benedict had lost track of the calendar. Shepherds who found him soon after, dressed in skins, first took him for an animal.

quote.exact: I know that it is Easter with me and a great feast, having found so much favour at God's hands as this day to enjoy your company
quote.display: I know that it is Easter with me and a great feast, having found so much favour at God's hands as this day to enjoy your company
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

life_moments.title: The nettles
life_moments.text: The memory of a woman he had once seen tormented him until he nearly left the wilderness. Instead he stripped and threw himself into a patch of briars and nettles and rolled there until he was torn. He later told his disciples he was never tempted that way again.

quote.exact: and so by the wounds of his body, he cured the wounds of his soul
quote.display: and so by the wounds of his body, he cured the wounds of his soul
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

life_moments.title: The poisoned wine
life_moments.text: Monks of a nearby monastery begged him to be their abbot. He warned them their ways and his would never agree, but gave in. When he held them to a strict life, they poisoned his wine. He made the sign of the cross and the glass flew apart. He told them to find an abbot who suited them and went back to his cave.

quote.exact: Go your ways, and seek ye out some other father suitable to your own conditions, for I intend not now to stay any longer amongst you.
quote.display: Go your ways, and seek ye out some other father suitable to your own conditions, for I intend not now to stay any longer amongst you.
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain
quote.note: The monastery is traditionally Vicovaro (Gardner's note 7: 'is said to have been').

life_moments.title: Twelve houses of twelve
life_moments.text: So many came to him that he built twelve small monasteries, each with a head and twelve monks, and kept a few with himself. Roman nobles gave him their sons to raise, among them Maurus and Placidus.

quote.exact: he built there twelve Abbeys; over which he appointed governors, and in each of them placed twelve monks
quote.display: he built there twelve Abbeys; over which he appointed governors, and in each of them placed twelve monks
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

life_moments.title: The jealous priest
life_moments.text: A local priest, Florentius, envied him. He slandered him, sent him a poisoned loaf, and sent seven naked young women to dance in the monks' yard. To protect his young monks, Benedict left with a few of them. Soon after, Florentius's room fell in and killed him. Benedict wept, and gave a penance to the monk who brought the news gladly.

quote.exact: he gave place to envy
quote.display: he gave place to envy
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

life_moments.title: Apollo's hill
life_moments.text: Above the town of Cassino, country people still worshipped Apollo in an old shrine among sacred woods. Benedict smashed the idol, overturned the altar and burned the woods. He built a chapel of St Martin in the temple and one of St John where the altar had been, and he preached until the people around became Christians. Here he built the monastery where he lived to the end.

quote.exact: The man of God coming thither, beat in pieces the idol, overthrew the altar, set fire to the woods, and in the temple of Apollo, he built the oratory of St. Martin, and where the altar of the same Apollo was, he made an oratory of St. John
quote.display: The man of God coming thither, beat in pieces the idol, overthrew the altar, set fire to the woods, and in the temple of Apollo, he built the oratory of St. Martin, and where the altar of the same Apollo was, he made an oratory of St. John
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain
quote.note: Year: Gardner's note 17 ('528 or 529'). The chapel of St Martin links to Martin's page.

life_moments.title: The king in disguise
life_moments.text: Totila, king of the Goths, wanted to test whether Benedict was a prophet. He dressed his sword-bearer Riggo in his royal robes and sent him with a guard of honour. Benedict called out before Riggo came near. Then Totila came himself and fell to the ground. Benedict lifted him up, rebuked him for his cruelty and told him how long he would reign.

quote.exact: Put off, my good son, put off that apparel, for that which thou hast on, is none of thine.
quote.display: Put off, my good son, put off that apparel, for that which thou hast on, is none of thine.
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain
quote.note: Latin: 'Pone fili, pone: hoc quod portas non est tuum.' Date: Britannica ('about 542'); Gardner's note 21 ('probably ... 542'); the Catholic Encyclopedia says 543 and calls it 'the only certain date we have in the saint's life'.

also.exact: Much wickedness do you daily commit, and many great sins have you done: now at length give over your sinful life.
also.display: Much wickedness do you daily commit, and many great sins have you done: now at length give over your sinful life.
also.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

life_moments.title: His sister's storm
life_moments.text: His sister Scholastica visited once a year. At the end of one day she begged him to stay and talk through the night. He refused: a monk may not stay out of his monastery overnight. She laid her head on her hands and prayed, and a storm broke from a clear sky so hard that no one could leave. Three days later, standing in his cell, he saw her soul rise to heaven like a dove. He had her buried in the grave he had made for himself.

quote.exact: God forgive you, what have you done?
quote.display: God forgive you, what have you done?
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

also.exact: I desired you to stay, and you would not hear me, I have desired our good Lord, and he hath vouchsafed to grant my petition
also.display: I desired you to stay, and you would not hear me, I have desired our good Lord, and He hath vouchsafed to grant my petition
also.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

also.exact: and therefore of right she did more which loved more.
also.display: and therefore of right she did more which loved more.
also.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain
also.note: Gregory's verdict. Latin: 'illa plus potuit, quae amplius amauit'.

life_moments.title: The whole world in one ray
life_moments.text: Praying at his window before dawn, he saw a light brighter than day. In it, he later said, the whole world was gathered before his eyes, and he saw the soul of Germanus, bishop of Capua, carried to heaven in a ball of fire. A messenger sent to Capua found that Germanus had died at that hour.

quote.exact: the whole world, gathered as it were together under one beam of the sun, was presented before his eyes
quote.display: the whole world, gathered as it were together under one beam of the sun, was presented before his eyes
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain
quote.note: Latin: 'sub uno solis radio collectus'. Gregory's explanation: the world did not shrink, 'but the soul of the beholder was more enlarged'.

life_moments_note: Eleven moments, all from Gregory; the death is its own section. Order follows Gregory's; only the Totila visit (about 542) has an outside date.

recorded.text: Yes, dozens. Book 2 is a book of wonders: 38 short chapters, almost every one a miracle, a prophecy or a vision. Gregory's own framing: saints work wonders sometimes by prayer, sometimes 'by power and authority', and he gives one of each (chapters 31 and 32).

pledge.exact: All the notable things and acts of his life I could not learn; but those few, which I mind now to report, I had by the relation of four of his disciples
pledge.display: All the notable things and acts of his life I could not learn; but those few, which I mind now to report, I had by the relation of four of his disciples
pledge.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain
pledge.note: Gregory's promise at the start; then he names the four.

items.title: The young monk under the wall
items.text: The devil told Benedict he was going to the monks at work, and Benedict sent a warning. Too late: a new wall fell and crushed a boy monk, the son of a town councillor. They carried him to Benedict in a sack, his bones broken. Benedict laid him where he himself prayed, sent everyone out, shut the door and prayed harder than ever. The same hour he sent the boy back to work on the wall.

quote.exact: for the very same hour he made him sound, and as lively as ever he was before; and sent him again to his former work
quote.display: for the very same hour he made him sound, and as lively as ever he was before; and sent him again to his former work
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

items.witness: The monks who carried him in and saw him go back to the wall.

items.title: The farmer's son
items.text: A farmer carried his dead son to the abbey gate and ran to find Benedict, crying 'Give me my son!' Benedict protested that such miracles were for the apostles, but the man swore he would not leave. Benedict knelt, lay on the child's body, rose and prayed with his hands raised to heaven. The child's body began to shake, and Benedict gave him back to his father alive.

quote.exact: Behold not, O Lord, my sins, but the faith of this man, that desireth to have his son raised to life, and restore that soul to the body, which thou hast taken away.
quote.display: Behold not, O Lord, my sins, but the faith of this man, that desireth to have his son raised to life, and restore that soul to the body, which Thou hast taken away.
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain
quote.note: Latin: 'ne adspicias peccata mea, sed fidem huius hominis, qui resuscitari filium suum rogat'.

witness.display: all which were present did behold it in strange manner to pant and shake
witness.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

note.display: Certain it is, Peter, that this miracle was not in his own power, for which prostrate upon the ground he prayed so earnestly.
note.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

more.title: The mended sieve
more.text: His nurse's borrowed sieve broke in two. He prayed with tears and it was whole.

quote.exact: that the place could not be seen where before it was broken
quote.display: that the place could not be seen where before it was broken
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

more.title: The glass that burst
more.text: He blessed the poisoned wine his monks offered him, and the glass broke.

quote.exact: the glass, that was holden far off, brake in pieces, as though the sign of the cross had been a stone thrown against it
quote.display: the glass, that was holden far off, brake in pieces, as though the sign of the cross had been a stone thrown against it

more.title: Water on the mountain
more.text: Three monasteries sat high on a rock and the monks tired of carrying water up. He prayed there at night and left three stones as a mark. The monks dug there and water came.

quote.exact: doth plentifully, even to this day, spring out and run down from the top to the very bottom of that hill
quote.display: doth plentifully, even to this day, spring out and run down from the top to the very bottom of that hill
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

more.title: The blade from the lake
more.text: A Goth clearing briars lost the iron head of his hook in the deep lake. Benedict put the handle in the water and the blade rose and fitted itself back on.

quote.exact: Behold here is thy bill again, work on, and be sad no more.
quote.display: Behold here is thy bill again, work on, and be sad no more.
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

more.title: Maurus on the water
more.text: Young Placidus fell into the lake and was swept out. Benedict sent Maurus, who ran out on the water, pulled him back by the hair, and only on shore realised what he had done.

quote.exact: A strange thing, and since the time of Peter the Apostle never heard of!
quote.display: A strange thing, and since the time of Peter the Apostle never heard of!
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

more.title: The raven and the loaf
more.text: A bird that came daily to be fed from his hand carried off the poisoned loaf Florentius had sent.

quote.exact: In the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, take up that loaf, and leave it in some such place where no man may find it.
quote.display: In the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, take up that loaf, and leave it in some such place where no man may find it.
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain
quote.note: P.W. writes 'crow'; the Latin is corvus, a raven.

more.title: Seeing from afar
more.text: He told monks back from an errand where they had eaten and how many cups they drank. He knew of a flask of wine hidden in a bush (a snake was in it) and of napkins a monk had slipped into his robe.

quote.exact: tell an untruth? for did you not go into such a woman's house?
quote.display: tell an untruth? for did you not go into such a woman's house?
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

more.title: Flour in a famine
more.text: With five loaves left, he told his monks they would have plenty tomorrow. Next morning 200 bushels of flour sat in sacks at his door, sent by no one anyone ever found out.

quote.exact: two hundred bushels of meal was found in sacks before his cell door
quote.display: two hundred bushels of meal was found in sacks before his cell door
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

more.title: The oil that overflowed
more.text: After the glass of oil was thrown from the window and did not break, he prayed with his monks beside an empty barrel. Oil rose until it lifted the lid and ran across the floor.

quote.exact: the oil within did so increase, that the cover began to be lifted up
quote.display: the oil within did so increase, that the cover began to be lifted up
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

more.title: Ropes loosed by a look
more.text: The Goth Galla's prisoner was freed when Benedict looked at his bonds (see 'hard to rattle').

quote.exact: whom the man of God, not with hands, but only with his eyes, had loosed from his bands
quote.display: whom the man of God, not with hands, but only with his eyes, had loosed from his bands
quote.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

doubt.title: Doubted then and now
doubt.text: Gregory himself marks what is second-hand: one prophecy about Rome, he says, his informant did not hear from Benedict's own mouth. His listener Peter keeps asking how such things can be. In the 1980s the historian Francis Clark argued that the Dialogues were not Gregory's at all, but a forgery of about 680. Most scholars were not persuaded.

quotes.exact: True it is that Honoratus, by whose relation I had this, saith not that he received it from his own mouth, but that he had it of other monks, which did hear it themselves.
quotes.display: True it is that Honoratus, by whose relation I had this, saith not that he received it from his own mouth, but that he had it of other monks, which did hear it themselves.
quotes.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

quotes.exact: as I must needs confess that in myself I never had experience of any such thing, so neither can I conceive by what means the whole world can be seen of any one man.
quotes.display: as I must needs confess that in myself I never had experience of any such thing, so neither can I conceive by what means the whole world can be seen of any one man.
quotes.source: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book 2, tr. "P.W." (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (1911), tertullian.org transcription, marked public domain

quotes.exact: Those not convinced by Clark's previous arguments won't, I suspect, be convinced by those offered in his new book.
quotes.display: Those not convinced by Clark's previous arguments won't, I suspect, be convinced by those offered in his new book.
quotes.who: Scott DeGregorio, reviewing Clark's second book (2003)

doubt.note: Clark's thesis in the reviewer's words: the Dialogues are 'not a late sixth-century work by that pope but a late seventh-century work by a forger'. Clark's books: The Pseudo-Gregorian Dialogues (Leiden: Brill; catalogues say 1987, the review says 1989) and The 'Gregorian' Dialogues and the Origins of Benedictine Monasticism (Brill, 2003). DeGregorio notes the Visio Baronti (about 678-79) already uses the Dialogues, 'suggesting, perhaps, that the traditional date of 593-94 is correct after all'. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1907) calls Book 2 'rather a character sketch than a biography' made 'for the most part, of a number of miraculous incidents'. Britannica: 'Though Gregory's work includes many signs and wonders, his outline of Benedict's life may be accepted as historical.' The 'Most scholars were not persuaded' sentence is supported by the review's tone and the Catholic and Britannica framing, not by a survey: soften to 'Clark's case has not won most scholars over' only if a checker wants it.

framing.text: He wrote one book, the Rule. Everything else he said comes through Gregory, who had it from his disciples. Label Rule lines 'from his Rule' and Dialogues lines 'as Gregory the Great recorded it'.

misquoted_or_legend.text: Claim: 'Ora et labora' (pray and work) is from his Rule, or was his motto. What the sources say: the words are not in the Rule (checked against the whole Latin text: no 'ora et labora'). Terrence Kardong, a monk and Rule scholar, writes that the phrase 'is found nowhere in the Rule of St. Benedict' and 'appears nowhere in Benedictine history before the 19th century', citing M.-B. Meeuws (Collectanea Cisterciensia 54, 1992), who traces it to a book by the German abbot Maurus Wolter. The Rule does balance prayer, reading and work (chapter 48). Pope Paul VI (1964) uses it as a saying about him ('secundum verba illa "ora et labora"').
misquoted_or_legend.source: Latin Rule (The Latin Library), searched by script; Kardong, 'Work Is Prayer: Not!' (OSB archive); Pacis nuntius
misquoted_or_legend.note: Meeuws's article was not opened; Wolter's 1880 book (Praecipua ordinis monastici elementa) is named in secondary sources only. Say 'first found in the 19th century' with Kardong as the source.

misquoted_or_legend.text: Claim: 'Always we begin again' is Benedict's. What the sources say: it is not in the Rule (checked in Verheyen and Hunter Blair) or in Gregory. It is the title of John McQuiston II's modern book 'Always We Begin Again: The Benedictine Way of Living', which its publisher calls his interpretation and restatement of the Rule.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Script search of the Rule (two translations) and Dialogues 2; Church Publishing (Morehouse) book page
misquoted_or_legend.note: The book's first year (1996) was not confirmed on the publisher page read. Do not print a year.

misquoted_or_legend.text: Claim: he founded the Benedictine Order. What the sources say: he founded single monasteries, each on its own under its abbot. The Catholic Encyclopedia speaks of 'His so-called order' and says 'a Benedictine may be more truly said to enter or join a particular household than to join an order'.
misquoted_or_legend.note: Merriam-Webster's own entry still says 'founder of Benedictine order': the looser usage is common.

misquoted_or_legend.text: Claim: Scholastica was his twin. What the sources say: Gregory calls her only 'his sister'. The twin story is a later tradition; the Catholic Encyclopedia: 'a tradition, which St. Bede accepts, makes him a twin with his sister Scholastica'. Britannica and the Episcopal Church repeat 'twin' as fact.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Dialogues 2, chapter 33 ('his sister called Scholastica'); Catholic Encyclopedia 1907; Britannica; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022
misquoted_or_legend.note: The Bede claim is the Catholic Encyclopedia's; where Bede says it was not traced.

misquoted_or_legend.text: Claim: the St Benedict medal and its prayer 'Vade retro Satana' are his. What the sources say: neither is in the Rule or in Gregory. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1912): 'It is doubtful when the Medal of St. Benedict originated'; its letters were found painted at Metten abbey in 1647 and explained by a manuscript 'written in 1415'; medals were first approved in 1741-42.
misquoted_or_legend.note: The search brief marks the medal itself 'not ours' (devotional); one plain line on the page is enough.

misquoted_or_legend.text: Claim: the briars he rolled in turned into roses. What the sources say: Gregory says nothing of it. Gardner's 1911 note: the thorns and nettles 'are piously said to have turned into the roses' still shown at the Sacro Speco.

Claim: every word of the Rule is his own invention. What the sources say: he drew on older writers, above all an anonymous 'Rule of the Master'. Britannica: 'a majority of competent scholars favor the earlier composition of the "Rule of the Master." If this is accepted, about one-third of Benedict's Rule (if the formal liturgical chapters are excluded) is derived from the Master.' His Rule ends by pointing readers to Cassian and 'the rule of our holy Father, Basil'.

Claim: the prayer 'Gracious and holy Father, give us wisdom to perceive You...' is his. What the sources say: it is not in the Rule (Verheyen, Hunter Blair) or in Gregory's Life (checked by script). Where it comes from was not traced.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Script search of the Rule and Dialogues 2
misquoted_or_legend.note: Only the negative is checked. Print only 'not in his Rule or in Gregory's Life', or leave the item out.

friends_family_rivals.text: Scholastica, his sister: dedicated to God from childhood, she visited him once a year; he saw her soul rise like a dove and buried her in his own grave.
His old nurse: followed him from Rome to Enfide and would not leave him; he slipped away from her to go to Subiaco.
Romanus, a monk nearby: gave him the monk's habit, kept his secret and fed him for three years.
Maurus and Placidus: sons of Roman nobles given to him as boys. Maurus became his right hand ('his master's coadjutor') and ran on the water to save Placidus.
The monks of Vicovaro: chose him as abbot, hated his strictness and poisoned his wine.
Florentius, a local priest: envied him, sent him a poisoned loaf and tried to corrupt his monks; Benedict left rather than fight, and mourned him when he died.
Totila, king of the Goths: tested him with a disguised servant, was rebuked to his face, and was told he would reign nine years.
friends_family_rivals.note: Gardner's note 21 on Gregory's bias: 'It was naturally impossible for St. Gregory to take an impartial view of the Goths, and modern historians depict Totila in far more favourable colours.'

friends_family_rivals.text: Servandus, deacon and abbot in Campania: a friend who came often for 'spiritual conference'; the only one Benedict called to see the light of his vision.
Theoprobus, a nobleman he converted: a close friend who found him weeping over the coming sack of his abbey, and whom he sent to Capua to learn of Germanus's death.

Gregory the Great: never met him. Gregory wrote his only early Life about fifty years after his death, from four of his disciples, and closed Book 2 with the line that Benedict 'could not otherwise teach, than himself lived'.
friends_family_rivals.source: Dialogues 2, prologue and chapter 8; site pair (people.benedict.pairs.gregory: 'Gregory the Great wrote the only early life of Benedict.')
friends_family_rivals.note: In chapter 8 it is Peter, not Gregory, who says Benedict was 'full of the spirit of all good men'; Gregory answers that he had the Spirit of the one true God.

summary.text: He foretold the day to his monks, near and far. Six days before, he had his grave opened. A fever took hold and grew worse. On the sixth day he had his monks carry him into the oratory, received the Body and Blood of Christ, and stood, held up by his disciples, with his hands raised to heaven. He died praying. The same day two monks, one in his cell and one far away, saw the same vision: a road hung with rich cloths and lit with lamps, running east from his cell to heaven.

later.text: A later story: that his bones were carried to Fleury in France in the 7th century. The Catholic Encyclopedia reports the dispute and Abbot Tosti's case that they are still at Monte Cassino. Gardner (1911): their bodies 'are supposed to lie together under the high altar of the abbey church at Monte Cassino; but this is a little uncertain'.

after.text: Gregory says his abbey was later sacked by the Lombards at night, and no monk was killed, as Benedict had foretold. Monte Cassino was destroyed again in the Second World War (1944) and rebuilt; Pope Paul VI consecrated the new church on 24 October 1964, the day he named Benedict patron of Europe.

not_a_martyr.text: He did not die a martyr. The 1916 Martyrology calls him 'the holy abbot'; Gregory's framing is of a man whose holiness showed in wonders and in his Rule.

oak.text: The site names him second among the Oak's kindred: 'As a young man he ran from praise and lived three years alone in a cave. When his own monks tried to poison him, he faced them “with a mild countenance and quiet mind”. When a raging Goth shouted at him to get up, the Goth ended at his feet, and Benedict “rose not up from his reading”.' Checks out: chapters 1, 3 and 31, both quotations word for word in P.W./Gardner.

hard_topics.text: Beatings in the Rule. The Rule lets the abbot punish the proud and disobedient with the rod 'at the very first offence' (chapter 2), orders stripes for monks who will not amend (chapter 28) and for boys who cannot grasp excommunication (chapter 30). Gregory shows Benedict striking a monk with a stick (chapter 4). The same Rule forbids anyone to strike a brother without the abbot's leave (chapter 70) and warns the abbot not to scrape the rust so hard that 'the vessel be broken' (chapter 64). Say both plainly.
hard_topics.source: Rule, chapters 2, 28, 30, 64, 70 (Hunter Blair and Verheyen); Dialogues 2, chapter 4
hard_topics.note: Hunter Blair, chapter 2: 'let him chastise with bodily stripes at the very first offence, knowing that it is written: The fool is not corrected with words.' Chapter 30: 'let them be punished by severe fasting or sharp stripes'. Holders' framing: the Rule calls the abbot 'a wise physician' who uses punishment only after admonition, and then adds 'what is still more powerful, his own prayers' (chapter 28). No public-domain critic's words were fetched; do not invent any.

hard_topics.text: He destroyed a pagan shrine. At Monte Cassino he smashed Apollo's idol, overturned the altar and burned the sacred woods (chapter 8). Gregory tells it as a victory; readers today may not. State it in Gregory's words.
A life written as a book of miracles, fifty years later, and its authorship questioned. See miracles.doubt: Gregory's own caveats, Clark's forgery thesis and DeGregorio's reply.

How original is the Rule? About a third may come from the anonymous Rule of the Master, if that rule is older, as most scholars now think (Britannica). The Episcopal essay: 'The major problem for historians is the question of how much of the rule is original.'

Gregory's Goths. The Goths in the Life are villains. Gardner (1911): 'It was naturally impossible for St. Gregory to take an impartial view of the Goths, and modern historians depict Totila in far more favourable colours.'
hard_topics.source: Gardner's note 21, in the tertullian.org text

hard_topics.text: Hard stories. Two nuns who would not stop insulting a man are seen, after death, leaving church at the dismissal of the excommunicated until Benedict sends an offering (chapter 23); a boy monk who left without a blessing is twice cast out of his grave (chapter 24). Tell them as Gregory tells them, or leave them out; do not soften them in our voice.

_checker_fixes_2026_09_25: Nurse: Gregory says 'his nurse' (Latin nutrix), never 'old'. Page now 'His nurse' (life moment 1, circle).
Poisoned wine (ch 3): he 'returned back to the wilderness which so much he loved' (Latin 'ad locum dilectae solitudinis'), not 'to his cave'.

Twelve monasteries (ch 3): Gregory does not call them small. Maurus was 'iunior' (a young man), Placidus 'puerilis adhuc indolis' (still a boy): not 'two boys'. Maurus 'magistri adiutor' = his helper, not 'right hand'.
Totila (ch 15): 'seeing him sitting afar off, he durst not come near, but fell down to the ground' (Latin 'sese in terram dedit'); Benedict came to him. Not 'fell at his feet'.
Scholastica (ch 33): they met 'not far from the gate, to a place that did belong to the Abbey' (Latin 'in possessionem monasterii'), not 'a house'.
Vision (ch 35): Benedict had Theoprobus dispatch the messenger; he did not send him himself.
Blade (ch 6): the Goth was 'poor of spirit' (pauper spiritu), i.e. humble, not a poor man.
Flour (ch 21): 'the next day', not 'the next morning'. Two nuns (ch 23): buried 'in the church' (in ecclesia), not 'their church'. Boy cast out (ch 24): 'loving his parents more than reason would'.

Temper trait: chapter 4 (the monk struck 'for the blindness of his heart' with 'a little wand') is not told as anger; dropped. Only chapters 25 and 28 say 'in anger' (iratus). Title now 'roused to anger'.
Moderate on purpose: 'a rule a beginner could keep' rests on chapter 73 ('this least rule written for a beginning'); cite now chapters 40, 64 and 73.
Sign your heart (ch 20): the monk is 'the son of a great man' (defensoris filius); Gregory does not say young.
Rule chapter 28: after prayer fails, 'let the Abbot dismiss him from the community'. The Punishment item now says so.
Boy under the wall (ch 11): Gregory names no witnesses; he says Benedict 'sent him again to his former work'. Witness line reworded.
Florentius (ch 8): the monk given the penance for rejoicing is Maurus, who sent the news. Named.

Clark: DeGregorio's review says Clark held the Dialogues 'albeit not by Gregory, nevertheless contain a significant amount of genuine Gregorian material' (about 25%). 'Not Gregory's at all' overstated it; reworded.
Theoprobus (ch 17): 'admonitione conversus' means turned to God (a devout life) at Benedict's urging, not necessarily brought to the Christian faith. Reworded.
In art: the white-bearded monk with a scroll is one fresco (Peć), so the page says so rather than 'In the East'.

Removed: 'Raised the dead 2' (the Miracles section's dark panel is the same number, '2 raised from the dead'); 'Rule chapters 73' (already under Wrote and in the lede of His Rule); 'Wine a day 1' (a hemina, an obscure unit; the wine line itself is quoted under His words); 'Rule read aloud 3' (the same facts are the Newcomers panel of His Rule); 'Patron of Europe 1964' (a year dressed up as a number, and told under Patron of, Is he a saint? and How he died). Four 'Did you know?' lines added. No picture added: the pictures column (portrait and personality box) ends 137px above the facts, less than any picture with its caption. Traits: two desktop rows swapped so the taller sits left ('hard to rattle' 274 before 'calm under attack' 200; 'gave the credit away' 200 before 'moderate on purpose' 176, the row above the lone 'ran from praise').

numbers.evidence: Dialogues, Book 2, chapter 1 (sources/people/benedict-of-nursia/gregory-dialogues-book2-pw1608-gardner1911.txt line 186): 'lived there in a strait cave, where he continued three years unknown to all men, except to Romanus'. Romanus fed him: the same chapter (the loaves let down on a rope, told in His life).

Dialogues, Book 2, chapter 3 (line 441): 'he built there twelve Abbeys; over which he appointed governors, and in each of them placed twelve monks'. At Subiaco, before he went to Monte Cassino (chapter 8).

Rule, chapter 18, tr. Verheyen (rule-verheyen-ccel.txt line 872): 'those monks show too lax a service in their devotion who in the course of a week chant less than the whole Psalter with is customary canticles; since we read, that our holy forefathers promptly fulfilled in one day what we lukewarm monks should, please God, perform at least in a week.'

tidbits.text: Joseph Ratzinger became Pope in 2005 and took the name Benedict ...
tidbits.evidence: Benedict XVI, General Audience, 27 April 2005 (fetched 2026-09-25 to sources/people/benedict-of-nursia/vatican-benedict-xvi-general-audience-2005-04-27.txt, from https://www.vatican.va/content/benedict-xvi/en/audiences/2005/documents/hf_ben-xvi_aud_20050427.html), line 76: 'I wanted to be called Benedict XVI in order to create a spiritual bond with Benedict XV, who steered the Church through the period of turmoil caused by the First World War. He was a courageous and authentic prophet of peace'; line 78: 'The name "Benedict" also calls to mind the extraordinary figure of the great "Patriarch of Western Monasticism", St Benedict of Norcia ... he is a fundamental reference point for European unity and a powerful reminder of the indispensable Christian roots of his culture and civilization.' Paraphrased, no quotation marks (the Vatican's text is not public domain).

tidbits.text: His monks sleep in their clothes, belted ...
tidbits.evidence: Rule, chapter 22, tr. Verheyen (rule-verheyen-ccel.txt line 938): 'Let them sleep clothed and girded with cinctures or cords, that they may be always ready; but let them not have knives at their sides whilst they sleep, lest perchance the sleeping be wounded in their dreams; and the sign having been given, rising without delay, let them hasten to outstrip each other to the Work of God'. CCEL page rule.xxiv.html is Chapter XXII (checked: its neighbours are XXI and XXIII).

tidbits.text: In Lent each monk gets a book from the library ...
tidbits.evidence: Rule, chapter 48 (line 1538): 'During these days of Lent let all receive books from the library, and let them read them through in order. These books are to be given out at the beginning of the Lenten season. Above all, let one or two of the seniors be appointed to go about the monastery during the time that the brethren devote to reading and take notice, lest perhaps a slothful brother be found who giveth himself up to idleness or vain talk, and doth not attend to his reading'. CCEL rule.l.html is Chapter XLVIII.

tidbits.text: The monk in charge of the stores must treat every pot and possession ...
tidbits.evidence: Rule, chapter 31, 'The Kind of Man the Cellarer of the Monastery Ought to Be' (line 1104): 'Let him regard all the vessels of the monastery and all its substance, as if they were sacred vessels of the altar.' CCEL rule.xxxiii.html is Chapter XXXI.
